patient.name: Gloria Adeyemi
patient.setting: GP home visit in January, then GP follow-up
patient.complaint: Sudden high fever, aching all over and a dry cough since last night
background: Missed her flu vaccine this autumn
Lives with her husband in Hackney
Several neighbours have had 'flu' this week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an abrupt winter fever, severe myalgia, dry cough and a normal chest; and questions on complications (secondary Staph. aureus pneumonia) and antigenic shift versus drift.

points: Gloria, 72: fine at teatime, shivering by 9 pm.
Too exhausted to get out of bed.

steps.lead: A winter outbreak among her neighbours and **abrupt** onset point to **influenza** A or B, spread by droplets.
Gloria's **age**, COPD and diabetes make her **high risk** for complications.

points: Chest: **clear**, no crackles, no bronchial breathing.

steps.lead: High fever, **severe myalgia**, dry cough and a **normal chest**: the classic early picture of flu.

steps.q: Gloria's neighbours are ill, onset was abrupt, myalgia severe and her chest clear. What is it?
steps.r: Abrupt fever with **severe myalgia** in a winter outbreak, normal chest: influenza. No anosmia (Covid) and no focal signs (pneumonia).

steps.title: Influenza vs common cold vs Covid-19
head: Feature
Influenza
Common cold
Covid-19

steps.lead: This winter's virus has **drifted**, which is why the vaccine is updated every year; a **shift** would cause a pandemic.
Gloria is told to call back if she gets **chest pain, breathlessness or worsening** after improving: possible secondary bacterial pneumonia.

visual.title: Chest X-ray if she had worsened (secondary pneumonia)
visual.caption: Right lower zone consolidation: **secondary bacterial pneumonia**, a complication. In simple flu the film is normal.

steps.text: What a secondary pneumonia would look like.
A clear chest does **not** argue against flu. Focal crackles and purulent sputum suggest a **secondary** pneumonia.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (nasopharyngeal swab for viral PCR), or no test when flu is circulating in a healthy adult.

steps.r: **Viral PCR** on a nasopharyngeal swab is the gold standard.

steps.lead: Gloria is high risk, so a **nasopharyngeal PCR** swab is sent; a healthy adult in peak season could be diagnosed clinically.

steps.text: The exam likes the healthy adult in **high community circulation**: no test needed, it is a clinical diagnosis.
Do not wait for the PCR result before giving an antiviral to a high-risk patient: start treatment on clinical suspicion.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?': supportive care for healthy adults, oral oseltamivir for high-risk patients, admission for IV antivirals in respiratory failure, and vaccination questions.

visual.title: Hours since symptom onset
visual.label: Gloria 20 h
visual.caption: Neuraminidase inhibitors work best **early** (NICE: within 48 hours); Gloria is well inside the window.

steps.q: Gloria has COPD and diabetes and is 20 hours in. What is first-line?
steps.r: High-risk patients get a **neuraminidase inhibitor**: oral oseltamivir (or inhaled zanamivir). Antibiotics do not treat a virus.

steps.lead: Gloria gets **oral oseltamivir** plus fluids, rest and paracetamol. Her healthy granddaughter would get supportive care only.

steps.title: Influenza management by risk
nodes: Healthy adult: rest, fluids, paracetamol or ibuprofen
High risk (comorbidity, immunosuppressed): oral oseltamivir or inhaled zanamivir
Respiratory failure: admit for IV antiviral

steps.lead: If Gloria's sats fell and her breathing quickened, she would be **admitted for IV antivirals**, and ICU if needed.

visual.title: Gloria's temperature on oseltamivir
visual.caption: Fever settles over days. A **second spike** after improvement would suggest secondary bacterial pneumonia.

steps.lead: Once recovered, Gloria (over 65 with chronic disease) must have her **annual flu vaccine**; it is postponed only while she is acutely unwell.
Gloria's vaccination falls under the **UK annual seasonal influenza programme** run by the JCVI and NHS.

steps.text: Zanamivir is **inhaled** and can cause bronchospasm: think twice in COPD or asthma. Oseltamivir is oral.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: how haemagglutinin and neuraminidase work (and why oseltamivir helps), antigenic shift vs drift, and why flu predisposes to Staph. aureus pneumonia.

steps.lead: The virus's **haemagglutinin** latched onto sialic acid on Gloria's airway cells; **neuraminidase** cuts new virions free. Oseltamivir blocks that release.

steps.title: Influenza life cycle and the drug target
nodes: New virions bud from the cell
Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid to release them

o: They prevent release of new virions
steps.r: Neuraminidase frees new virions; blocking it traps them on the cell surface and **limits spread**.

steps.lead: Small **point mutations** (drift) cause each winter's epidemic; **reassortment** between strains (shift) creates a pandemic subtype.

steps.title: Antigenic drift vs shift
head: Feature
Drift
Shift
rows: Point mutations in H and N

steps.lead: Flu strips Gloria's ciliated epithelium, impairing **mucociliary clearance** and opening the door to Staph. aureus or Strep. pneumoniae.

steps.text: The **segmented** RNA genome is what makes reassortment, and so antigenic shift, possible.

mcq.q: Which feature is most characteristic of influenza?
What is the classic secondary bacterial cause of pneumonia after influenza?
What is the chest examination usually like early in influenza?
What is the gold-standard test for influenza?
What class of drug is oseltamivir?
What should you do with the flu vaccine if a patient is acutely unwell?
Why does influenza predispose to bacterial pneumonia?

technique.stem: A 46 year old man has had a sudden onset of fever, severe aching in his back and legs, headache and dry cough since yesterday. It is January and several colleagues are off work with similar symptoms. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His chest is clear.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Abrupt high fever, **severe myalgia**, winter outbreak, clear chest.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cough after a cold with mild fever; not abrupt prostration.
Mild, gradual, coryza; not high fever and severe myalgia.
Would give focal signs; his chest is clear.
Young adults, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, over weeks.

steps.x: **E. Influenza.** Rule: abrupt fever + severe myalgia + winter outbreak + normal chest = flu.

technique.stem: A 68 year old woman with chronic kidney disease has had a sudden fever, myalgia and dry cough for 1 day during a winter outbreak. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 134/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

clues: sudden fever, myalgia and dry cough
steps.x: Suspected flu in a high-risk patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Looks for complications, does not diagnose flu.

steps.x: **C. Nasopharyngeal swab for viral PCR.** Rule: flu gold standard = **nasopharyngeal swab PCR**.

technique.stem: A 59 year old man with diabetes has had influenza for 3 days. He is now increasingly breathless and drowsy. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87% breathing air. Influenza A PCR is positive.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: He is in respiratory failure; home treatment is unsafe.
Antibiotics do not treat flu, and he needs admission.
Right for stable high-risk patients, not respiratory failure.
Supportive care alone is unsafe here.

steps.x: **A. Admit for intravenous antiviral therapy.** Rule: flu with respiratory failure = **admit for IV antivirals**, ICU if needed.

technique.stem: A new influenza A subtype emerges after a pig farmer is infected with human and swine strains at the same time. It spreads rapidly worldwide because very few people have immunity.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?

clues: human and swine strains at the same time

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Gradual point mutations; seasonal outbreaks, not pandemics.

steps.x: **B. Antigenic shift.** Rule: shift = reassortment = pandemic; drift = mutations = seasonal.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman developed fever, shivering, severe muscle aches and a dry cough over a few hours yesterday. It is February and her children were ill last week. Her temperature is 39.3°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Her chest is clear.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Abrupt high fever, severe myalgia and dry cough in winter with a clear chest is influenza; Covid-19 would suggest anosmia.

steps.x: Diagnosis: abrupt febrile illness in winter.
Abrupt high fever, severe myalgia, contacts, clear chest.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Follows a cold, mild fever, rhonchi.
Anosmia would be the clue; onset is more gradual.
Sore throat, exudate, nodes; not severe myalgia and cough.

steps.x: **C. Influenza.** Rule: abrupt + severe myalgia + winter = flu.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man had influenza a week ago and was improving. He now has a high fever, cough productive of purulent sputum and breathlessness. His temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 120 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows bilateral cavitating lesions.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Secondary bacterial pneumonia after influenza is classically Staphylococcus aureus, which causes cavitation.

steps.x: Organism question: secondary pneumonia after flu.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: COPD exacerbations; does not typically cavitate after flu.
Water exposure, hyponatraemia; not post-flu cavities.

steps.x: **E. Staphylococcus aureus.** Rule: post-flu pneumonia, especially cavitating = **Staph. aureus**.

practice.stem: A 33 year old man has had influenza for 5 days. He now has central chest pain and palpitations. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 106/70 mmHg. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia with widespread T-wave inversion.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: Chest pain, tachycardia, raised troponin and widespread T-wave changes after flu in a young man is myocarditis, a recognised complication.

steps.x: Complication question: heart involvement after flu.
Viral illness, chest pain, raised troponin, widespread changes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Young, no risk factors, viral prodrome.
Pleuritic pain, reduced breath sounds; troponin not raised.
Hypoxia and leg signs; troponin can rise but viral myocarditis fits.

steps.x: **C. Myocarditis.** Rule: flu + chest pain + raised troponin in a young adult = **myocarditis**.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman has had influenza-like illness for 2 days, with fever, myalgia and dry cough. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest examination?
o: Bronchial breathing at the left base
Reduced breath sounds with stony dullness
practice.e: In early uncomplicated influenza the chest examination is usually normal; crackles suggest secondary bacterial pneumonia.

steps.x: Most likely finding: what does early flu look like?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

steps.x: **C. Normal breath sounds.** Rule: early flu = **normal chest**; focal signs mean a complication.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant has had abrupt fever, severe myalgia, headache and dry cough for 1 day during a winter outbreak. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 106 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Her chest is clear.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Abrupt fever, severe myalgia and dry cough in a winter outbreak is influenza; pregnancy makes her high risk.

steps.x: Abrupt febrile myalgic illness, pregnant (high risk).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Uterine tenderness and offensive discharge; no cough.
Anosmia would be expected; myalgia and abrupt onset fit flu.
Pleuritic pain, hypoxia, no high fever and myalgia.

steps.x: **C. Influenza.** Rule: pregnancy is a **risk factor**; the picture is still flu.

practice.stem: A 75 year old man who had his influenza vaccine last year develops influenza this winter. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. The circulating strain has small changes in its haemagglutinin compared with last year's.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his infection despite vaccination?
practice.e: Antigenic drift, gradual point mutations in haemagglutinin and neuraminidase, evades last year's immunity and requires annual vaccine updates.

steps.x: Explanation question: small changes in surface antigens.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Shift is a new subtype causing a pandemic.
The standard IM vaccine is inactivated.

steps.x: **A. Antigenic drift.** Rule: drift = small changes, seasonal outbreaks, **annual vaccine update**.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man with heart failure has had sudden fever, myalgia and dry cough for 1 day. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Nasopharyngeal swab for viral PCR is the gold standard for influenza.

clues: sudden fever, myalgia and dry cough

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

steps.x: **D. Nasopharyngeal swab for viral PCR.** Rule: gold standard = **viral PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab**.

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman has had abrupt fever, severe myalgia and dry cough for 1 day. There is high community circulation of influenza. She has no medical history. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: During high community circulation influenza can be diagnosed clinically in healthy adults; PCR is for high-risk or uncertain cases.

steps.x: Investigation: does this healthy adult need a test?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Gold standard, but not needed in a healthy adult during high circulation.

steps.x: **D. No investigation, clinical diagnosis.** Rule: high circulation + healthy adult = **clinical diagnosis**.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease has had abrupt fever, myalgia and dry cough for 24 hours during a flu outbreak. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: High-risk patients (diabetes, CKD) get oral oseltamivir first-line; IV antivirals are for respiratory failure.

clues: type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: For respiratory failure; she is stable.
Does not treat a viral infection.
Right for healthy adults, but she is high risk.

steps.x: **D. Oral oseltamivir.** Rule: high risk = **oral oseltamivir** (or inhaled zanamivir).

practice.stem: A 31 year old man has had abrupt fever, myalgia and dry cough for 2 days during a flu outbreak. He has no medical history. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. His chest is clear.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Uncomplicated influenza in a healthy adult needs bed rest, fluids and analgesia; antivirals are for high-risk patients.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

steps.x: **E. Rest, fluids and paracetamol.** Rule: uncomplicated flu in a healthy adult = **supportive care**.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man with COPD attends a flu vaccination clinic. He has had a fever of 38.4°C and a productive cough since yesterday. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate action regarding his vaccination?
o: Give a live attenuated vaccine instead
Postpone vaccination until he has recovered
practice.e: Vaccination is postponed while acutely unwell, then given because he is ≥65 with chronic disease.

steps.x: Vaccination question: what if acutely unwell?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Not used in adults this age; still postpone.
He is in a priority group (≥65, COPD).

steps.x: **E. Postpone vaccination until he has recovered.** Rule: **postpone** flu vaccine if acutely unwell; never drop it.

practice.stem: A 64 year old woman with influenza A is prescribed oseltamivir. A student asks how the drug works.
practice.q: Which is the mechanism of action of oseltamivir?
o: Blocks haemagglutinin binding to sialic acid
Inhibits neuraminidase, preventing release of new virions
practice.e: Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase, which normally frees new virions from the host cell, so spread is limited.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No drug in this class blocks entry.

steps.x: **D. Inhibits neuraminidase, preventing release of new virions.** Rule: oseltamivir/zanamivir = **neuraminidase inhibitors**.

prompts.q: What is influenza, and how is it spread?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the virus type and genome.

points.p: Acute viral respiratory infection by influenza A or B
Enveloped virus with segmented RNA genome
Respiratory droplets and close contact, mainly winter

prompts.q: Who is at risk of severe influenza?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: these are also the antiviral and vaccine groups.

points.p: Older age
Chronic disease
points.why: Heart, lung, kidney, liver, neuro, diabetes.

points.p: Pregnancy
Immunosuppression

prompts.q: Describe the classic presentation and examination of influenza.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: abrupt, severe myalgia, normal chest.

points.p: High fever and severe myalgia
Dry cough, headache, fatigue, sore throat
Exam: fever, tachycardia, chest usually normal initially

prompts.q: What is the difference between antigenic shift and antigenic drift?

points.p: Shift: novel H/N subtype, little immunity: pandemics
Drift: gradual mutations: seasonal outbreaks

prompts.q: What are the complications of influenza?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: secondary pneumonia is the big one.

points.p: Secondary bacterial pneumonia, commonly Staph. aureus
Sinusitis, otitis media
Myocarditis
Pulmonary embolism
Chest pain, breathlessness or hypoxia = suspect secondary pneumonia (emergency)

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: PCR, or clinical in season.

points.p: Gold standard: nasopharyngeal swab for viral PCR
Clinical diagnosis in healthy adults during high community circulation

prompts.q: How is influenza treated, by risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: risk and severity decide.

points.p: Uncomplicated: rest, fluids, paracetamol or ibuprofen
High risk: oral oseltamivir (Tamiflu) or inhaled zanamivir
Respiratory failure: admit for IV antivirals
ICU for mechanical ventilation if needed

prompts.q: Who should have the annual flu vaccine, and what are the rules?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: priority groups and postponement.

points.p: Age ≥65, chronic disease, healthcare workers, pregnant women, contacts of immunosuppressed
Standard IM vaccine is inactivated, safe in comorbidities
Postpone if acutely unwell until recovered

prompts.q: How does influenza enter and leave cells, and why do neuraminidase inhibitors work?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: H in, N out.

points.p: Haemagglutinin binds sialic acid receptors (entry)
Neuraminidase releases new virions; blocked by oseltamivir/zanamivir

prompts.q: Why does influenza predispose to bacterial pneumonia, and how does shift happen?

points.p: Epithelial destruction impairs mucociliary clearance
Classically Staph. aureus or Strep. pneumoniae
Shift: reassortment of gene segments between strains (e.g. human/animal)

glossary.influenza: Acute viral respiratory infection caused by influenza A or B virus.
glossary.segmented RNA genome: A viral genome split into separate RNA pieces, which can swap between strains.
glossary.enveloped: A virus wrapped in a lipid membrane taken from the host cell.
glossary.prostration: Extreme exhaustion that stops someone getting out of bed.
glossary.haemagglutinin: Influenza surface protein that binds sialic acid to let the virus enter cells.
glossary.neuraminidase: Influenza surface enzyme that cleaves sialic acid to release new virions.
glossary.sialic acid: Sugar on host cell surfaces that influenza haemagglutinin binds.
glossary.virions: Complete virus particles that can infect other cells.
glossary.antigenic drift: Gradual point mutations in H and N causing seasonal epidemics and annual vaccine updates.
glossary.antigenic shift: Reassortment between strains creating a novel subtype with pandemic potential.
glossary.reassortment: Swapping of gene segments when two influenza strains infect the same cell.
glossary.pandemic: A new infection spreading worldwide because few people are immune.
glossary.oseltamivir: Oral neuraminidase inhibitor (Tamiflu) for high-risk patients with influenza.
glossary.zanamivir: Inhaled (or IV) neuraminidase inhibitor; can cause bronchospasm in asthma or COPD.
glossary.neuraminidase inhibitor: Antiviral class that stops new influenza virions leaving infected cells.
glossary.PCR: Polymerase chain reaction: detects viral genetic material; gold standard for influenza.
glossary.nasopharyngeal swab: Swab taken from the back of the nose to test for respiratory viruses.
glossary.Staph. aureus: Staphylococcus aureus: bacterium that classically causes severe, cavitating pneumonia after flu.
glossary.Strep. pneumoniae: Streptococcus pneumoniae: the commonest cause of community-acquired pneumonia.
glossary.mucociliary clearance: Cilia sweeping mucus and trapped microbes out of the airways.
glossary.secondary bacterial pneumonia: Bacterial lung infection that follows a viral illness such as flu.
glossary.myocarditis: Inflammation of the heart muscle, sometimes after viral infection.
glossary.cavitating: Forming air-filled holes within lung consolidation.
glossary.JCVI: Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation, which advises the UK on vaccines.
glossary.inactivated vaccine: Vaccine made from killed virus; cannot cause infection.
glossary.aTIV: Adjuvanted trivalent influenza vaccine, offered to people aged 65 and over.
glossary.respiratory failure: Low blood oxygen (with or without high CO2) because the lungs cannot exchange gas well enough.
glossary.COPD: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: fixed airflow obstruction, usually from smoking.
